questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A simplified form that was already a character
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a simplified glyph borrowed from an older character
questions.stem: Item 0001: A board note asks which simplified shape had already served as a full character before the reform; choose the best reading.

options.text: It shows the reform reused characters that already carried the meaning.
It shows some simplified forms were borrowed from existing characters.
options.misconception: assumes all simplified forms were newly invented

options.text: It shows the reform only renamed old glyphs and never reduced strokes.
It shows simplified forms are identical to traditional forms always.

questions.explanation: Some simplified shapes existed as independent characters earlier, so the reform borrowed rather than invented every form. The tempting idea that reform only renamed glyphs mistakes borrowing for renaming.
questions.hint: Look for reuse of an existing character.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Two traditional characters with one simplified form
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two traditional characters share one simplified form
questions.stem: Item 0002: Explain why two traditional characters sometimes collapse into one simplified form and what risk that creates for readers.

answer.exemplar: Two traditional characters collapse into one simplified form when the reform merges variants that shared meaning or pronunciation, and the risk is that readers lose the distinction between originally separate words in older texts.

questions.explanation: Merging variants reduces stroke counts but erases historical distinctions. The tempting shortcut of treating the merge as pure simplification ignores the lost contrast between the two originals.
questions.hint: Think about what information the merge removes.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Adding up the simplified character table
questions.learningObjective: Count simplified characters from a small table

stimulus.body: A board table lists four simplified characters with stroke counts 3, 5, 7, and 9. The planner asks for the total stroke count if each is written once.

questions.stem: Item 0003: What is the total stroke count when the four listed simplified characters are written once each?

options.text: The total is 20 strokes because 3 plus 5 plus 7 plus 9 equals 24 minus 4.
The total is 24 strokes from adding 3, 5, 7, and 9 directly.
The total is 26 strokes because the table header adds two strokes.
The total is 22 strokes because one character is counted twice.

questions.explanation: Adding 3, 5, 7, and 9 gives 24 strokes. The tempting errors come from inventing header costs or double counts that the table does not contain.
questions.hint: Add the four given stroke counts directly.

questions.topic: The three tiers of the modern standard list
questions.learningObjective: Name the three tiers of the modern standard list
questions.stem: Item 0004: Which option first names the three tiers of the modern standard list and then explains their purpose?

options.text: The tiers are first, second, and third, and they rank characters by dictionary order.
options.misconception: ranks by dictionary order instead of usage

options.text: The tiers are old, middle, and new, and they rank characters by reform date.
options.misconception: ranks by reform date instead of usage

options.text: The tiers are small, medium, and large, and they rank characters by stroke count.
options.misconception: ranks by stroke count instead of usage

options.text: The tiers are common, frequent, and rare, and they rank characters by daily usage.

questions.explanation: The modern standard list groups characters by frequency of use into common, frequent, and rare tiers. The other options invent ranking schemes that the standard does not use.
questions.hint: Think about how often characters appear in daily text.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: How much of the everyday set was simplified
questions.learningObjective: Estimate the share of the everyday set that was simplified
questions.stem: Item 0005: A note claims most of the everyday set was simplified; which statement best checks that claim?

options.text: It is true because every common character received a simpler stroke form.
It is false because only a minority of common characters changed form.
It is true because simplified forms always replace traditional forms everywhere.
It is false because no common character was ever simplified.

questions.explanation: Only a minority of the everyday set was simplified, so claiming most changed overstates the reform. The tempting extremes of all or none both misread the actual scope.
questions.hint: Compare the number changed with the total everyday set.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Where a one-to-one correspondence breaks
questions.learningObjective: Spot where a one-to-one mapping between forms breaks
questions.stem: Item 0006: Explain where a one-to-one correspondence between traditional and simplified forms breaks and why it matters.

answer.exemplar: A one-to-one correspondence breaks when one simplified form maps to multiple traditional characters, so a single simplified glyph can hide two distinct original meanings for readers of older texts.

questions.explanation: When one simplified form covers several traditional characters, the mapping stops being one-to-one. The tempting assumption that every simplified glyph has exactly one traditional partner fails in those cases.
questions.hint: Look for a simplified form with more than one traditional partner.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why mainland and other regional standards print different shapes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why regional standards print different shapes

stimulus.body: A board note compares two printed samples of the same character from different regional standards. The shapes differ slightly in stroke endings and component placement.

questions.stem: Item 0007: Why do mainland and other regional standards print slightly different shapes for the same character?

options.text: Because printers in one region always omit the final stroke of every character.
Because one region uses simplified forms and the other uses traditional forms only.
options.misconception: confuses regional shapes with simplification levels

options.text: Because each region codified its own preferred stroke endings and component placement.
Because the character has no standard form in either region.
options.misconception: denies the existence of standard forms

questions.explanation: Regional standards encode different preferred stroke endings and component placement, producing visibly different shapes. The tempting simplification-versus-traditional explanation confuses regional variation with script level.
questions.hint: Focus on codified stroke and component preferences.

questions.topic: A simplified form that was already a character
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish borrowed simplified forms from newly created ones
questions.stem: Item 0008: Which option both identifies a borrowed simplified form and explains how to verify it?

options.text: A borrowed form is always printed in bold; verify by checking font weight.
options.misconception: uses font weight as the test

options.text: A borrowed form always has fewer than five strokes; verify by counting strokes.
options.misconception: uses stroke count as the test

options.text: A borrowed form is always a radical; verify by isolating its left part.
A borrowed form appears in older dictionaries; verify by checking its earlier standalone use.

questions.explanation: A borrowed simplified form can be traced to earlier standalone use in dictionaries. Stroke count, radical status, and font weight are not valid tests of borrowing.
questions.hint: Check historical standalone use in reference works.

options.misconception: mistakes a one-to-one row for a merge

options.text: Row two maps two traditional characters to a single simplified form.
Row three maps one simplified character to two traditional stroke counts.
options.misconception: confuses stroke counts with character counts

options.text: Row four maps a simplified form to a pronunciation table entry.

questions.explanation: A merged pair appears when two traditional characters share one simplified form, as in row two. The other rows describe one-to-one mappings or unrelated tables.

questions.topic: Adding up the simplified character table
questions.learningObjective: Compute an average stroke count from a table
questions.stem: Item 0010: Explain how to compute the average stroke count of five simplified characters given their individual counts.

answer.exemplar: To compute the average stroke count, add the five individual stroke counts together and divide the sum by five, rounding only at the end to avoid losing precision.

questions.explanation: The average requires summing all five counts and dividing by five. Rounding intermediate values early would distort the result, which is the common tempting error.
questions.hint: Sum first, then divide by the count of characters.

questions.learningObjective: Match a character to its tier by frequency

stimulus.body: A board table shows three characters: one appears in daily newspapers, one in academic texts, and one only in specialized dictionaries. The planner must assign each to a tier.

questions.stem: Item 0011: Which character belongs to the rare tier?

options.text: The character appearing in daily newspapers belongs to the rare tier.
The character appearing in academic texts belongs to the rare tier.
The character appearing only in specialized dictionaries belongs to the rare tier.
All three characters belong to the rare tier because they are all listed.

questions.explanation: The rare tier holds characters that appear only in specialized dictionaries, not daily or academic text. Daily and academic characters fall into common or frequent tiers.
questions.hint: Rarity follows how seldom a character appears in everyday reading.

The two counts are equal, so exactly half changed.
The unsimplified count exceeds the simplified count, so most characters stayed unchanged.

questions.explanation: The unsimplified count exceeds the simplified count, so most everyday characters stayed unchanged. The tempting reversal or even split misreads the actual proportions.

questions.stem: Item 0013: Which case breaks a one-to-one correspondence between traditional and simplified forms?

options.text: A case where one traditional character maps to one simplified character.
A case where a character is never simplified at all.
A case where one simplified form maps to two traditional characters.
A case where a character keeps the same stroke count after reform.

questions.explanation: The mapping breaks when one simplified form covers two traditional characters. Unchanged characters and equal stroke counts do not break the correspondence.

questions.stem: Item 0014: Explain the source of regional shape differences in printed characters.

answer.exemplar: Regional shape differences stem from distinct codified standards that prescribe stroke endings and component placement, so the same character can look slightly different across regions.

questions.explanation: Each region follows its own codified standard for strokes and components, producing visible differences. The tempting idea of random printer variation misses the standardization behind the shapes.
questions.hint: Think about codified standards, not printer variation.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a borrowed form matters for lexicography

stimulus.body: A board note lists a simplified form that also appears as an independent entry in an older dictionary. The planner must decide how this affects dictionary cross-references.

questions.stem: Item 0015: What does the borrowed status of a simplified form imply for dictionary cross-references?

options.text: Cross-references should merge all entries into one regardless of history.
Cross-references should delete the older entry because it is obsolete.
Cross-references should ignore the older entry and list only the new form.
Cross-references should link the simplified form to its older independent entry.

questions.explanation: A borrowed simplified form should link to its older independent entry in cross-references. Deleting or ignoring that entry loses the historical standalone use.
questions.hint: Preserve the link to the older independent entry.

questions.stem: Item 0016: Which option first identifies the confusion risk of a merged form and then proposes a remedy?

options.text: The risk is larger file size; the remedy is compressing font data.
The risk is slower handwriting; the remedy is practicing strokes more.
The risk is misreading old texts; the remedy is checking context or older dictionaries.
The risk is fewer characters overall; the remedy is adding new characters.

questions.explanation: The real risk of a merged form is misreading older texts, and context or older dictionaries help disambiguate. Handwriting speed, file size, and character count are not the core risk.
questions.hint: Focus on reading comprehension of older texts.

questions.stem: Item 0017: A table sums to 30 strokes; which check confirms the sum?

options.text: Divide the row counts and confirm the quotient equals 30.
Multiply the row counts and confirm the product equals 30.
Subtract the row counts and confirm the difference equals 30.
Re-add the row counts and confirm they equal 30.

questions.explanation: The sum is verified by re-adding the row counts. Multiplication, subtraction, and division are the wrong operations for checking a total.

questions.topic: The three tiers of the modern standard list
questions.learningObjective: Explain why tiers use frequency rather than strokes
questions.stem: Item 0018: Explain why the modern standard list tiers characters by frequency rather than by stroke count.

answer.exemplar: The tiers use frequency because a character's usefulness in daily reading matters more than its stroke count, so common characters are prioritized regardless of how simple they look.

questions.explanation: Frequency reflects real reading need, while stroke count does not. The tempting assumption that simpler characters are more common conflates visual simplicity with usage.
questions.hint: Usefulness in daily reading drives the tiering.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage of the everyday set simplified

stimulus.body: A board note states that 500 of 2000 everyday characters were simplified. The planner must express this as a percentage.

questions.stem: Item 0019: What percentage of the everyday set was simplified?

options.text: 20 percent, from dropping the trailing zero in 500 over 2000.
25 percent, from 500 divided by 2000 times 100.
40 percent, from 2000 divided by 500.
5 percent, from 500 divided by 10000.

questions.explanation: 500 divided by 2000 equals 0.25, so 25 percent of the everyday set was simplified. The wrong options misplace decimals, invert division, or change the denominator.
questions.hint: Divide simplified count by total count, then convert to percent.

questions.stem: Item 0020: Which option first notes a broken mapping and then states its encoding consequence?

options.text: A broken mapping means traditional forms are no longer readable.
A broken mapping means every character needs a new code point immediately.
A broken mapping means one code point may represent two historical characters, complicating search.
A broken mapping means simplified forms should be abolished.

questions.explanation: A broken mapping means one code point can represent two historical characters, which complicates search and retrieval. Universal recoding, readability loss, and abolition are overreactions.
questions.hint: Focus on search and retrieval ambiguity.

questions.explanation: Different stroke endings reflect different codified regional standards, not typesetting errors. The character still has accepted forms in each region.

Multiply the known row counts and divide by the total to recover the missing value.
Subtract the known row counts from the total to recover the missing value.
Set the missing value to zero because it was not listed.

questions.explanation: The missing value is recovered by subtracting known row counts from the total. Multiplication, guessing, and assuming zero are invalid methods.

Learners may overcount strokes in the simplified form.
Learners may conflate two distinct traditional meanings under one simplified glyph.

questions.explanation: The key risk is that learners conflate two distinct traditional meanings under one simplified glyph. Motor memory, stroke counting, and total rejection are secondary or unfounded.
questions.hint: Focus on meaning conflation.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a form counts as simplified

stimulus.body: A board note lists a character whose simplified form is identical to an older independent character. The planner must decide whether it counts as simplified.

questions.stem: Item 0043: Should this form count as simplified?

options.text: No, because a borrowed form cannot be a simplified form.
Yes, because it functions as the simplified form in the modern standard even though it pre-existed.
Yes, but only if it has fewer strokes than the traditional form.
No, because the modern standard does not list it.

questions.explanation: A borrowed form still functions as the simplified form in the modern standard, so it counts. Excluding borrowed forms or adding stroke conditions misclassifies it.
questions.hint: Function in the standard matters, not origin.

answer.exemplar: Borrowed forms teach that the reform combined preservation with reduction, reusing older characters where possible rather than inventing every simplified glyph from scratch.

questions.explanation: The reform preserved existing glyphs where useful while reducing strokes elsewhere. Pure invention or pure preservation would both misdescribe it.

Set the missing row to zero and report the total as complete.
